newsitem.title: UK: First UK gilt sale of financial year set to appeal.
newsitem.headline: First UK gilt sale of financial year set to appeal.

text.p: The Bank of England will start the 1996/97 financial year in style on Wednesday with a five-year gilt auction which analysts say is likely to be gobbled up.

The Bank will sell two billion stg of 7.0 percent gilts due 2002. Traders had expected the Bank to try and ship out either 2.5 or 3.0 billion pounds of stock, so a mere two billion should prove no trouble.
"They could have got away with selling a bit more than that," said Steve Scott, gilts analyst at Kleinwort Benson. He expected the auction to attract cover of more than two times.
Five-year gilt auctions tend to be well received. An auction of the same stock in January received bids totalling a staggering 3.82 times more than the 1.5 billion pounds of stock on offer.
Scott said the five-year part of the gilt curve had underperformed 10-years recently as investors switched longer.

That cheapening also leaves the stock well positioned to be snapped up. "These short maturity gilts have cheapened up recently and with only 2.0 billion stg for sale the auction should not be a problem," said Joanne Collins, bond analyst at Nomura.
One fly in the ointment for overseas investors may be the election, due in just nine days.

But with a Labour victory seemingly cut-and-dried -- the party is still at least 15 points ahead in most opinion polls -- even that should not prove too much of an obstacle. "People feel there's good value there but obviously in a week before an election there's some uncertainty," said Darren Winder, economist at SBC Warburg. "But I would be surprised if there was cover of less than two."

Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW, said the auction stock has long been trading at a special rate in the repo market, which suggests plenty of pent up demand. "Much of the stock seems to be in the hands of overseas investors who are not lending it out, so there should be good demand on Wednesday."

A final piece in the jigsaw of a successful auction would be a soft retail sales number. Official March sales data will be released at 0830 GMT on Wednesday, less than two hours before the auction results are announced.

Economists forecast a modest 0.3 percent rise in sales, for a 4.3 percent year-on-year rise. Any suggestion that consumer demand is not accelerating would ease fears of sharp interest rate rises after the election.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said on Monday he was not convinced interest rates need to rise. Clarke told BBC Radio there was no sign of consumer demand accelerating. He said factory gate prices remained subdued and the strong pound "was having an effect."
But if the polls are right, it will be Labour's Gordon Brown, not Clarke, who has the keys to the Treasury after May 1.
